The Ruddy-tailed flycatcher (Terenotriccus erythrurus) is a small tyrant flycatcher for which several key life-history parameters have been estimated from comparative data. Neonates emerge from their eggs after an incubation period of approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] when maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a relatively brief developmental window typical of many small-bodied passerines. The wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.5 grams [Wwb = 0.5 grams], a figure derived from allometric relationships within the Onychorhynchidae. This diminutive starting mass, reflecting the limited yolk reserves of a small egg, places the species among the lighter hatchlings of its clade, setting the stage for a rapid growth trajectory under the warm, humid conditions of its understory habitat where insect prey is abundant and predation pressure on nestlings is high.

Sexual dimorphism becomes readily apparent as individuals approach their asymptotic body size. Adult females ultimately attain a wet body mass of approximately 6 grams [Wwi = approximately 6 grams], while adult males are consistently heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of around 7 grams [Wwi = around 7 grams]. This 1-gram disparity in adult mass is modest but consistent with the species' breeding ecology, where males may not require a size advantage for territory defense. Under a stable thermal regime characteristic of the active metabolic period at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum lifespan for this species has been recorded at approximately 2,482 days [am = approximately 2,482 days], a longevity figure that reflects the relatively high survivorship of adult tropical passerines compared to their temperate counterparts.

Under the warm thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic phase, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the species displays a predictable schedule of developmental milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of first sustained flight, occurs at 9 days after hatching [tx = 9 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid nest departure is characteristic of many small-bodied insectivorous birds that rely on concealment rather than prolonged brooding to avoid predation. Following fledging, juveniles continue to receive parental care for a period before achieving full nutritional independence, gradually refining their foraging skills in the dense forest understory.

The onset of reproductive capability also unfolds under these warm conditions. Puberty, marked by full gonadal maturation, is reached at 27 days after hatching [tp = 27 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at this thermal regime, indicating that individuals can potentially breed within their first year if ecological conditions permit at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Furthermore, first reproduction, defined as the time since birth at first brood, occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the same thermal conditions, suggesting that while gonadal development is rapid, actual breeding is typically deferred until the following breeding season at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Reproductive output in this species appears constrained by its small body size. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing 2 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 2 eggs]. This modest annual fecundity is compensated for by extended longevity. Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials indicate a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 43.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 43.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a rate consistent with the high metabolic demands of such a small endotherm and reflecting the energetic costs of maintaining homeothermy in a humid tropical environment.
